Evaluation of health literacy in lung transplant 
candidates 
Jorge Vinales, BS,a,1 Rommel Sagana, MD,b,2 Kiran H. Lagisetty, MD,c,3  
Corey Powell, PhD,d,4 Jeffrey Clay, ADN,e,5 Rebecca Hunt, BSN,e,6

KEYWORDS: 
lung transplantation; 
health literacy; 
education  
Understanding health literacy is critical to making informed decisions in healthcare. To date, there are 
no studies regarding the landscape of health literacy in patients undergoing lung transplant evaluation. 
In this single center prospective pilot study, patients undergoing evaluation for lung transplantation 
participated in a pre-transplant education class followed by an educational assessment administered 
electronically. The Brief Health Literacy Screening Tool (BRIEF) was then electronically administered 
to assess health literacy among patients. Thirty patients participated. Most patients (77%) demonstrated 
adequate health literacy. The pre-transplant education assessment score and BRIEF survey scores 
correlated (R=0.43 [95% CI 0.06–0.70, P =0.025]). Inadequate/marginal health literacy was seen in 
13% (2/16) of patients listed for transplant and 36% (5/14) of patients not listed for transplant (p=0.37).

Introduction 
Health literacy is critical to making informed decisions in 
healthcare. For patients undergoing evaluation for life- 
saving procedures such as lung transplantation, under­
standing the information presented to them in the pre- 
transplant evaluation phase is important for informed de­
cision making. Low health literacy in the general adult 
population has been associated with poorer health outcomes

including increased hospitalizations, decreased ability to 
take medications correctly and difficulty interpreting health 
messages.1 In the elderly, low health literacy has been as­
sociated with higher mortality rates. In patients undergoing 
evaluation for kidney transplantation, 8.9% of candidates 
had limited health literacy and those with limited health 
literacy had a 30% decreased chance of being listed for 
transplant and 2.42-fold increased risk of waitlist death.2 
To date, there is no data evaluating health literacy in 
patients undergoing evaluation for lung transplantation. The 
purpose of this study is to identify the prevalence of limited 
health literacy in lung transplant candidates using the Brief 
Health Literacy Screening (BRIEF) tool and identify risk 
factors associated with marginal/inadequate health literacy. 
Materials and methods 
This was a single center prospective pilot study of adult (18 
years or older), English speaking participants undergoing 
evaluation for lung transplantation between 2022 and 2024. 
Participants eligible were those who completed the pre- 
transplant education class and the education assessment, 
which is an electronic internal assessment distributed to all 
patients covering key pre-transplant concepts. An electronic 
survey using the BRIEF tool was electronically sent to 
participants to assess health literacy status. The BRIEF tool 
is a 4-item self-reported instrument that uses categorical 
scoring, with scores ranging from 2–20. Scores between 
2–12 indicated inadequate health literacy, 13–16 indicated 
marginal health literacy and 17–20 indicate adequate health 
literacy.3 It has been validated against two other measures 
of health literacy assessments including the shortened Test 
of Functional Health Literacy in Adults (s-TOHFLA) and 
the Rapid Estimate of Adult Literacy in Medicine 
(REALM).3 Participation in the BRIEF survey was volun­
tary. Full survey instruments are available in supplemental 
information (S1, S2). This study was reviewed by the in­
stitutional review board (HUM00227401). 
Categorical demographic and outcome variables were 
summarized using frequencies and percentages and con­
tinuous variables using means and standard deviations or 
medians and interquartile ranges. Fisher’s exact tests and T- 
tests were used to assess associations between categorical 
variables and health literacy, defined as marginal/in­
adequate or adequate, and between continuous variables 
and health literacy, respectively. Confidence intervals were 
calculated, and the Pearson correlation was tested between 
the transplant education quiz score and the BRIEF survey 
score based on the R function cor.test. Analysis of variance 
was incorporated to consider the association between the 
transplant equation quiz score and health literacy among 
respective categories: inadequate, marginal, and adequate. 
R version 4.3.1 was used for statistical analysis. 
Results 
A total of 40 participants completed the pre-transplant edu­
cation class/assessment and 30 responded to the BRIEF 
survey (response rate = 75%). Among the 10 non-responders, 
at the time of data analysis, 2 patients had a closed evalua­
tion, while the remainder had an open evaluation. Among 
survey responders, the majority were Caucasian, female, and 
completed education beyond high school (64%) (Table 1). 
The primary indication for lung transplant was non-idio­
pathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) interstitial lung disease (ILD) 
(37%). Among non-responders, the majority were Caucasian 
(80%), middle age (median 61 years), female (50%), and 
completed high school education (50%). 
The median baseline health literacy score (IQR) was 18 
among all patients. Twenty-three (77%) had an “adequate” 
health literacy status (Score > 16), while 3 (10%) had “mar­
ginal” (Score 13–15) and 4 (13%) had “inadequate” status 
(Table 2). Most patients scoring in the “adequate” range 
completed education beyond high school (74%). There was no 
significant association between health literacy status and any 
other covariates analyzed (Table 1). Furthermore, there was no 
significant difference in pre-transplant comorbidities between 
different health literacy groups (Table 1). 
The pre-transplant education assessment score and 
BRIEF survey scores correlated (R=0.43 [95% CI 
0.06–0.70, P =0.025]). Of those who completed the BRIEF 
Survey, 16 (53%) have been listed for transplant. Two 
(13%) participants listed for transplant demonstrated mar­

ginal/inadequate health literacy compared to 5 (36%) 
participants who were not listed for transplant (p=0.37) 
(Figure 1). Moreover, of those who were listed, 11 (69%) 
received a transplant and all of them displayed an “ade­
quate” health literacy status. 
Discussion 
While the impact of patients’ health literacy has been de­
scribed in renal, cardiac and liver transplantation, this is the 
first study to describe the baseline health literacy and

explore risk factors associated with poor health literacy in 
patients undergoing lung transplant evaluation.4–7 The 
majority of patients in our study demonstrated adequate 
health literacy, however, nearly 1 in 4 patients had marginal 
or inadequate health literacy. This finding suggests that like 
the adverse events associated with low health literacy 
highlighted by other solid-organ transplant studies, a sig­
nificant cohort of patients undergoing evaluation for lung 
transplant may also be at risk. Furthermore, the only de­
mographic variable associated with “adequate” health lit­
eracy was education beyond high school and, of those 
patients who received a transplant, all displayed “adequate” 
health literacy. This finding elucidates the probable asso­
ciation between health literacy and the likelihood of un­
dergoing transplant. Although the driving factors behind 
this association are beyond the scope of this paper, previous 
studies have shown that health literacy is positively asso­
ciated with medication adherence, pointing to a potential 
factor.8 Additionally, the majority of the patients who 
completed the pre-transplant assessment and BRIEF survey 
were white, meaning that they account for the majority of 
patients undergoing evaluation for transplant at our single 
institution. While this discrepancy may be specific to our 
institution’s geographic location, previous studies have 
shown lower referral rates for renal transplant evaluation in 
black patients when compared to their white counterparts.9 
This discrepancy points to the importance of addressing 
racial inequalities in healthcare to ensure more equitable 
outcomes. 
The main limitation of our study was the small sample 
size drawn from a single center. While our sample size is 
limited by the number of lung transplant evaluations per­
formed at our institution, we are working to create a multi­
center partnership to not only increase the number of patients 
involved in our study, but also to diversify our patient po­
pulation. In doing so, we believe we will be able to better 
assess the risk factors associated with low health literacy in 
patients undergoing transplant and ultimately optimize edu­
cational content for patients with any given health literacy 
status. Addressing disparities in health literacy has shown 
improved outcomes in other diseases and our study is the first 
to demonstrate a health literacy gap among patients under­
going lung transplantation evaluation.10
